question: A 7-year-old child with nutritional rickets has bilateral severe genu varum. Medical treatment with vitamin D and calcium has been started. When is the correct time to perform corrective osteotomy for the lower limb deformities?

answers.text: Immediately, to prevent further deformity progression during growth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Operating before metabolic correction is a serious error. Active rickets means the bone is poorly mineralised — osteotomies through such bone heal poorly, and the deformity will recur as the growth plate continues to be affected by the underlying metabolic disease.

answers.text: After 3–6 months of medical treatment, regardless of biochemical response

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Timing is not simply a matter of waiting 3–6 months. Biochemical normalisation (Ca, PO4, ALP returning to normal) must be confirmed first. In resistant (e.g., X-linked hypophosphataemic) rickets, this may take considerably longer.

answers.text: After full biochemical correction of the metabolic disease AND after the child reaches skeletal maturity (growth plate closure)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Surgical correction is deferred for two reasons: (1) operating through poorly mineralised rickets bone risks non-union and recurrence; (2) spontaneous remodelling after metabolic correction is substantial during growth — many deformities correct without surgery once the disease is treated. Osteotomy is reserved for residual deformity at or near skeletal maturity.

answers.text: Corrective osteotomy is never indicated in rickets — deformities always resolve with medical treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While many deformities do improve with medical treatment, some residual deformities — particularly severe angular deformities in X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets — require corrective osteotomy. However, this is done after biochemical correction and at or near skeletal maturity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the 'medical first, surgery last' rule for rickets deformities. Operate only after (1) confirmed biochemical correction and (2) skeletal maturity — both conditions must be met. Premature surgery leads to poor healing and deformity recurrence.

Key principle: in rickets, NEVER rush to surgery. Correct the metabolic disease first (confirm with biochemistry), allow for spontaneous remodelling during growth, and reserve osteotomy for persistent deformity at skeletal maturity.
